f1-emuA:
First the reason not to. This is serious. The Global Ayahuasca Survey came out recently. In short physical and mental adverse effects are common, severely so not so common, context matters. It’s real and these medicines can open things up faster than one might be able to support, let alone a group.

These medicines also attract people who want what they have to reveal but are not willing to do the work. People will come wanting to collect experiences / ceremonies / origin stories etc etc. If the primary purpose is to provide a great peak experience, it will be a problem when someone can’t figure out how to apologize to their housemate.

On the other hand, in my experience there are huge benefits to these medicines being used in a communal setting. Psychedelics allow people to drop the defenses that would normally enter into conversations like this. They can be extremely binding, but can also create all sorts of issues with maturity, grandiosity, dependency and general interaction. Is the community mature enough to handle this?
f1-emuB:
One of the reasons not to have medicine as part of a community, as many of the physical and psychological negative effects of ayahuasca (found in the global ayahuasca survey ) are quite common, although severe effects are far less common and highly contextualised. In other words the medicine can open people up faster than they can deal with it.

The medicines also attract people who like the revelatory aspects of the medicine but don’t want to do the work. In fact they’ll often collect as many ceremonies and stories of how they came to know the medicine as they can, but still struggle to say sorry to their housemate when they’ve fucked up. If the community attracts people for primarily that reason, then it’s gonna be a bit shit.

On the other hand, having used these medicines communally myself, they can be great for overcoming the defence mechanisms people put up which dominate conversation, create really powerful bonds between community members, but can also create confusion, grandiosity, dependency and other problematic ways of being with others. It’s a question of how mature the community is to deal with that stuff.
f2-emuA:
I won’t go down the path of the need or lack thereof of shamans (I know that’s a contentious one with many lineages and schools of Ayahuasca and Bwiti) but,

I do think it’s dangerous to promote any person as more to be listened to than your own experience. When you’re in a potentially vulnerable situation, opening yourself up more and more, what if that person is just a charismatic nutcase who’s never been held accountable by anyone and is floating around the retreat circuit? What if they’re a sexual predator? What if they’re financially invested in you coming back again and again? What if they’re just plain wrong?
f2-emuB:
Note: I don’t believe in “special” shaman, which is in opposition to most lineages, especially in ayahuasca and Bwiti.

The thing I’m referring to here is giving a single person, usually charismatic, more authority than your own experience. This can be a big problem when people follow a certain person in the retreat circuit. That person might be a truly wise human being, but they might also be someone who hasn’t been vetted, someone who is not held accountable, a sexual predator, someone who benefits financially from you needing them, or someone who is wrong about the things they’re saying. And the stakes are higher when people are opening up.
f3-emuA:
It’s very common that people have a longing after a deep psychedelic or mystical experience to find their tribe, to make a village, and to help bring others to this place.

I know this calling. And I know the illusion of self-importance that can come with this. It is so easy to come back from this place and think that you can love everyone into health, and then to come into contact with people who don’t want to change, or who say they want to change but can’t stop doing what they need to stop, or who have a serious crisis.

So, while the calling may be real, it’s not a great idea to make a village if you are still coming from this place of omnipotence.

Also a group tends to expand too fast, and take on too many people, and commit to doing too much when they are in a state of collective spiritual euphoria. It’s better to wait until you can do the math, and until you have a few people who are depending on you, to read the sections about making a village and about becoming a member in a village, further down in this article.

Once the euphoria wears off, and you still feel the calling, then it can be a good idea to make a village, to learn more about what you need to do, and to be with people who can support you, and eventually to make a new village. This, by the way, is an answer to the accusation that making a commune is a way to get out of the world, to stop dealing with the world, and to take advantage of the world.
f3-emuB:
Quite a few people have a desire to form a village after some deep psychedelic or mystical experiences. There’s a strong urge to get to know “your people”, and to help others to get where you have.

I know this urge. And I know the omnipotent tendency to grandiosity that can go along with it. “I can help anybody with love.” And then you run into the people who don’t want to change, or don’t even know they need to change. And you run into the people who want to change, but who regularly choose the opposite. And you run into the people who need more help than you are capable of giving.

It’s possible that the call is real, but it’s a bad idea to form a village while you’re in that state.

Other than the usual problems of new groups getting euphoric and taking on more people than they can handle, or thinking they can help more people than they actually can, or not realizing how much help they might need until someone needs it, there are a couple of other things to be aware of. See the sections on Capacity , and on Being Part of a Village , later in this article.

After the euphoria wears off, and the “call” matures a bit, it can be a great thing. One of the functions of a place like this is to give people a place to learn about this stuff and then go off and form their own villages. That also deals with one of the common objections to this whole idea, that people are just forming little communities to get away from the world.
